newsitem.title: USA: Tense atmosphere at White House leads to handshake.
newsitem.headline: Tense atmosphere at White House leads to handshake.

text.p: The first sign that President Bill Clinton's Middle East summit was not a flop came when Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu shook hands without Clinton playing matchmaker.

Things got better when Netanyahu and Arafat were coaxed into having a lunch of pan-roasted chicken and couscous together in the White House library, from where Franklin Roosevelt broadcast his fireside chats.
The sunny autumn day began tinged with an atmosphere of tense uncertainty. It was unclear what to expect from two leaders whose forces spilled blood on the West Bank and Gaza Strip only a week ago.
As the limousines arrived, heavy security blocked Pennsylvania Avenue in front of the White House. The front lawn was crowded with television crews preparing for a long day of live news coverage.

White House aides worried about putting Arafat and Netanyahu together too soon. They set up a careful route for each to follow through the warren of West Wing rooms to ensure they did not did not have an awkward meeting in a hallway.
In the lobby outside the Oval Office stood bodyguards for Netanyahu and Arafat.
U.S. officials found Netanyahu and Arafat more willing to talk to each other than expected.

When it was time for the group meeting between Clinton, Netanyahu, Arafat and Jordan's King Hussein, Clinton sent U.S. Middle East coordinator Dennis Ross into the Roosevelt Room where the leaders awaited their escort into the Oval Office.

Ross' mission was to "check the temperature" to see if Clinton might need to coax a handshake between Netanyahu and Arafat for photographers. Clinton was mindful of his 1993 role in persuading Arafat and the late Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin to shake hands during a Rose Garden ceremony.
What Ross found, said White House spokesman Mike McCurry, was that Arafat and Netanyahu "had clearly shaken hands and exchanged greetings."

Once they were all in the Oval Office, King Hussein made an emotional appeal to them to honour their prior commitments to peace, explaining how he prays five times a day for peace and that Netanyahu and Arafat should do the same.
Netanyahu and Arafat, sitting opposite each other on yellow couches, addressed each other at times, and spoke to the group at other times.
With the goal in mind of getting Netanyahu and Arafat to sit down together alone to hash out their differences, Clinton and King Hussein suggested the group have lunch.

In a carefully choreographed scene, the four men trooped side by side out of the Oval Office to the diplomatic entrance of the White House, as the cameras whirred. Arafat was spotted adjusting his headdress.
Once ensconced in the library, Clinton and King Hussein got up after 20 minutes, leaving Netanyahu and Arafat alone with interpreters.
Staff for each side had lunch in the China Room next door. The two leaders had met face-to-face only once before, about a month ago in a Gaza border town.

As the meeting stretched into late afternoon, a clearly relieved McCurry said it was important for the two leaders to "establish a personal relationship that allows them to deal very honestly and very forthrightly with the differences that do exist."
